title: (Principal-level) You designed the system: what evidence would make you change your architecture? If you recommend Redis, explain what would convince you it is unnecessary. If you chose async messaging, explain what would make synchronous communication preferable. If you proposed microservices, identify which assumptions justify the boundaries: and why is an architecture much easier to trust when the engineer who designed it can also describe the conditions under which it becomes the WRONG architecture?
shortTitle: What evidence would make you change your architecture?
keyPoints: Every architectural choice rests on assumptions about load, latency, data volume, team structure, and failure modes.
A principal-level engineer can state the specific, measurable evidence that would invalidate each choice.
Redis is unjustified when cache hit rate is low, the DB has spare read capacity, or the data fits in an in-process cache.
Async messaging is wrong when the caller needs an immediate authoritative answer or cannot tolerate eventual consistency.
Microservice boundaries are wrong when most features require coordinated deploys, one team owns everything, or services share a database.
An architecture is easier to trust when the designer states its own falsification conditions: it proves the choice was reasoned, not fashionable.
Good architecture is a time-bound fit to current constraints; the designer's job includes marking the expiry conditions.

s1_definition.oneliner: A trustworthy architecture comes with its own falsification conditions -- the designer can state the measurable evidence that would make each choice wrong, which proves it was reasoned, not fashionable.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Falsification Conditions** – specific, measurable evidence that would invalidate an architectural choice and trigger a redesign.
- **Redis Justification** – assumes a hot set read far more than written, high enough read volume that the DB cannot cope, and latency gain worth the operational cost.
- **Async Messaging Justification** – assumes the caller does not need an immediate authoritative result and can tolerate eventual consistency.
- **Microservice Boundaries Justification** – assumes independent scaling, deployment, and ownership along genuine domain seams with low cross-boundary coupling.
- **Epistemic Humility** – the ability to describe conditions under which your own design becomes wrong, proving it was evidence-based.
- **Architecture Decision Record (ADR)** – pairs each assumption with the condition that would invalidate it, reviewed against live metrics on a cadence.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India decides to open a new express counter, a good branch manager does not just say "express counters are good." They say "I am opening this because more than one in three customers only need a quick balance check; if that drops below one in ten, this counter is wasting a clerk and I will close it." That second sentence -- the condition under which the decision becomes wrong -- is what makes the manager trustworthy.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Architecture Falsification Framework
  ─────────────────────────────────────

  For each decision:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Decision: Use Redis for balance cache  │
  │                                        │
  │ Assumptions:                           │
  │   • Hit rate > 80%                     │
  │   • DB read utilization > 60%          │
  │   • Latency gain justifies cost        │
  │                                        │
  │ Falsification triggers:                │
  │   • Hit rate < 60% → remove Redis      │
  │   • DB util < 30% → remove Redis       │
  │   • Data < 100MB → use Caffeine        │
  │                                        │
  │ Review: quarterly against live metrics  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Trustworthy architecture = decision + its own expiry conditions
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The mark of principal-level thinking is not confidence in a design but the ability to state precisely what would prove it wrong. Every architectural choice rests on assumptions, and the professional move is to make those assumptions explicit with measurable triggers.

If you recommend Redis, the falsification is a low cache hit rate or a database with spare read capacity. If you chose async messaging, the falsification is a use case needing an immediate authoritative answer. If you proposed microservices, the falsification is that most features require coordinated deploys and one team drowns in distributed overhead.

An architecture is much easier to trust when the designer states its own falsification conditions, because it proves the choice was reasoned from evidence, gives concrete triggers to revisit, and builds trust with reviewers. Good architecture is a time-bound fit to current constraints, and the designer's job includes marking the expiry conditions so the system evolves deliberately.

Remember one sentence: a trustworthy architecture comes with its own falsification conditions, because an engineer who can describe when their design becomes wrong proves it was reasoned, not fashionable.
